content.text: The sky is blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight contains every color, each traveling as electromagnetic waves of different wavelengths. As sunlight passes through the atmosphere, it interacts with gas molecules—mostly nitrogen and oxygen—that are much smaller than the wavelength of visible light. This scattering is strongly wavelength-dependent, scaling roughly as 1/λ⁴. Shorter wavelengths, like blue and violet, scatter nearly ten times as much as longer red ones. So when you look away from the Sun, you see blue light redirected toward your eyes from all directions, while red light mostly travels straight through—which is also why sunsets look red. The sky isn't violet, though: the Sun emits less violet light, and human eyes are less sensitive to it, so the combined light we perceive reads as pale blue.
